title: Problems Around Polynomials — Problem 3
exact_target: How many isolated common real zeros can a sum of squares of bounded-degree polynomials have?
definition_tex:
\subsection{Definitions and mathematical statement}
Fix integers $k,\ell\geq1$. Consider polynomials $P\in
\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_\ell]$ of total degree exactly $2k$ admitting a
representation
\[
 P=Q_1^2+\cdots+Q_s^2,\qquad
 s\geq1,\quad Q_j\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_\ell],\quad \deg Q_j\leq k.
\]
The number $s$ is unrestricted and may depend on $P$. Such a polynomial
is nonnegative on real space, and its real zero set is exactly the
common real zero set of all the $Q_j$.

A zero $a$ is isolated if a neighborhood of $a$ contains no other common
zero. Let $Z_{\mathrm{iso}}(P)$ count these distinct real points, and put
\[
 N_{\mathrm{SOS}}(k,\ell)
   =\sup_P Z_{\mathrm{iso}}(P).
\]
Positive-dimensional components may coexist with the isolated zeros;
they do not contribute to the count. Neither complex zeros nor
projective points at infinity are counted.

Determine this extremal function for arbitrary $k$ and $\ell$, including
sharp upper bounds and constructions attaining them. A basic lower
bound is $k^\ell$: take one summand
$Q_j=\prod_{s=1}^{k}(x_j-s)$ for each coordinate $j$.
The question concerns all sums of squares, including representations
with more summands than variables, rather than only square systems
of $\ell$ equations. Consequently a count obtained for a generic
complete intersection does not by itself establish an upper bound
for this class. This is the general extremal problem, separate from
any proposed closed formula for its answer.

\subsection{Short English statement}
How many isolated common real zeros can a sum of squares of bounded-degree polynomials have?
